did_you_know.text: Did you know? This verse teaches that no one can be certain about tomorrow, so it is wise to avoid boasting and arrogant plans for the future: “For you do not know what a day may bring.”
Did you know? Proverbs values praise spoken by someone else over self-praise: “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth.”
Did you know? The chapter emphasizes that a fool’s anger can be heavy and burdensome, more than a physical load, and it also warns of the destructive power of wrath, fury, and jealousy.

Did you know? According to Proverbs, open and honest rebuke may be better than love that remains hidden; moreover, the wounds of a friend are trustworthy, while an enemy’s kisses are excessive and deceptive.

Did you know? This verse shows how feelings of fullness or hunger affect our perception of taste: a person who is full rejects even honey, while someone who is hungry may find sweetness in something bitter.

Did you know? A person who wanders from home is compared to a bird that wanders from its nest; the image highlights the bond between a person and their place, as well as the need for belonging and a home.

Did you know? The chapter praises maintaining loyal relationships with a friend and with one’s father’s friends, teaching that in times of need, a nearby neighbor may be more helpful than a brother who is far away.
Did you know? A son’s wisdom brings joy to his father’s heart and enables him to answer those who insult him; wisdom is presented here both as a source of joy and as a defense of the family’s honor.

Did you know? Just as the person who tends a fig tree is rewarded by eating its fruit, so the one who serves and cares for their master is rewarded with honor; the verse connects sustained responsibility with reward.

Did you know? The closing verses call on people to know the condition of their flocks and herds well, because wealth and status are not permanent; pasture, wool, meat, and goat’s milk are presented as practical sources of livelihood.
